title: Read a Digital Input
description: Read a pushbutton's state using digitalRead(), and print it to the Serial Monitor.

steps.clip: Grab an Arduino Uno and its USB cable, a breadboard, a pushbutton, one 10 kΩ resistor and a few jumper wires.
Push the button into the breadboard so it sits across the middle gap: two legs above the gap, two below.
hints: The two legs in the same column — one above the gap, one below — are always connected inside the button.
Pressing the button connects its left column to its right column.
steps.goal: Put the button across the middle gap.

steps.clip: Take a jumper wire. Put one end in a free hole in one of the button's columns — either one — and the other end into the 5V pin on the Arduino.
hints: 5V is on the Arduino's power header, next to the GND pins.
Any free hole in that column works.
steps.goal: Connect one side of the button to 5V.

steps.clip: Take another wire. Put one end in the button's other column (the one without the 5V wire) and the other end into pin 2 on the Arduino.
hints: It's the column on the other side of the button from the 5V wire.
When you press the button, 5V flows through it into pin 2.
steps.goal: Connect the other side of the button to pin 2.

steps.clip: Now the resistor. Put one leg in the same column as the pin 2 wire, and the other leg in an empty column.
hints: A resistor works either way round.
This is a pull-down resistor: it keeps pin 2 at 0 V (LOW) while the button isn't pressed.
steps.goal: Add the 10 kΩ resistor to the pin 2 side of the button.

steps.clip: Take one more wire from the resistor's other leg (the one in the empty column) to a GND pin on the Arduino.
hints: Any GND pin on the Arduino works — they're all connected inside the board.
steps.goal: Connect the other end of the resistor to GND.

steps.clip: Upload the code, then open the Serial Monitor. It shows 0 while the button is up and 1 while you hold it down.
